title: Erdős #1: Structural Theory of Distinct Subset Sums
description: Structural foundations for Erdős Problem #1 (Distinct Subset Sums). Proves the superincreasing extension lemma (the key construction principle), establishes that powers of 2 always yield DSS sets, proves DSS existence for any n (filling the gap in OQ03's minDSSBound), and derives elementary structural constraints: all elements must be positive, and the total sum satisfies sum(A) ≥ 2^n − 1.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. All results are fully proved in Lean 4.
originalContributions: dss_superincreasing_extend: If A has DSS and b > sum(A), then insert b A has DSS (the key structural lemma)
powers_of_two_has_dss: {1,2,4,...,2^(n-1)} has distinct subset sums for any n (inductive proof via superincreasing)
dss_exists: For any n, there exists an n-element set with DSS (existential witness for minDSSBound)
not_dss_of_mem_zero: If 0 ∈ A, then A does NOT have DSS (∅ and {0} give same sum)
dss_elements_pos: All elements of a DSS nonempty set are positive
dss_subset: Any subset of a DSS set also has DSS (monotone property)
dss_sum_lower_bound: sum(A) + 1 ≥ 2^n for any n-element DSS set A
minDSS_witness: Fills the sorry in OQ03's minDSSBound definition

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #1 (1931, $500 prize) asks whether any set of n positive integers with all 2^n subset sums distinct must have maximum element ≥ c · 2^n. The current gallery formalizes the counting bound (OQ01), the DFX entropy framework (OQ02), the Conway-Guy sequence (OQ03), and extremal sets (OQ04). This WIP extension adds the foundational structural theory that underlies all these results.
overview.problemStatement:
If A ⊆ ℕ has the distinct subset sums property (∀ S T ⊆ A, sum(S) = sum(T) → S = T), what structural constraints must A satisfy? In particular:
1. When can we extend A while preserving DSS?
2. What is the canonical construction giving DSS sets of any size?
3. What are the necessary conditions on elements?
overview.proofStrategy:
The central tool is the **superincreasing extension lemma**: if A has DSS and b > sum(A), then A ∪ {b} has DSS. The proof is by case analysis on whether b is in each of the two subsets:
- Both contain b: subtract b from both sums, apply DSS of A.
- b in one but not the other: the sum with b is > sum(A), while the sum without is ≤ sum(A). Contradiction.
- Neither contains b: both subsets lie in A; apply DSS of A directly.

From this lemma, powers of 2 give DSS (by induction: 2^n > ∑_{i<n} 2^i), and existence for any n follows immediately.
keyInsights: The superincreasing extension lemma is the constructive core of all known DSS constructions. Both the Conway-Guy sequence and the powers-of-2 sequence are superincreasing, which is why they have DSS.
0 cannot be in a DSS set: ∅ and {0} would both have sum 0 but be distinct subsets. This forces all elements positive.
The sum lower bound sum(A) ≥ 2^n − 1 (for n-element DSS A) is derived from the injective pigeonhole argument: 2^n subset sums in [0, sum(A)] forces 2^n ≤ sum(A) + 1.
The DSS monotone property (any subset of a DSS set has DSS) means the problem has a hereditary structure — the DSS 'language' is an antichain under inclusion.

conclusion.summary: This file provides the structural foundations for Erdős Problem #1: the superincreasing extension lemma (the construction principle behind all known DSS sets), the powers-of-2 DSS construction (proved by induction), existence of DSS sets for any n (filling the sorry in OQ03), positivity of elements, and the global sum lower bound. All results have 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The superincreasing lemma gives a recursive DSS construction: start with A = {} and repeatedly add any element larger than the current sum. This shows DSS sets are not 'rare' — they can be built greedily. The powers-of-2 construction is the smallest such greedy sequence. The Conway-Guy sequence (OQ03) is a more efficient greedy strategy that nearly achieves the conjectured optimal constant c = 1/(2π^{1/2}) ≈ 0.28.
openQuestions: Erdős $500 conjecture: must max(A) ≥ c · 2^n for some absolute c > 0?
What is the exact constant c? Upper bound c ≤ 0.22009 (Conway-Guy 1968).
Is the Conway-Guy sequence optimal? (Open for n > 10)
